title.en: The man who signs but does not rule

text.en: A state in India has two heads, a Governor who signs the papers and a Chief Minister who leads the government. Understanding who holds which power is the heart of how a state is run.

India has 28 states and 8 Union Territories, and Part VI of the Constitution, Articles 152 to 237, gives all states a uniform structure of government.
The State Government has three branches, the Executive, the Legislature and the Judiciary.
The Governor is the constitutional head of the state executive, and Article 154 vests the executive power of the state in him.
He is appointed by the President for a usual term of five years, holds office at the pleasure of the President, and generally does not belong to the state.
To be Governor one must be an Indian citizen of at least 35 years, not a member of Parliament or any legislature, and not hold any profitable post.
Executive powers: he appoints the Chief Minister, the ministers on the Chief Minister's advice, and members of the State Public Service Commission.
He is chancellor of the state universities and rules the state directly when President's Rule is imposed.
Legislative powers: he summons and prorogues the legislature, dissolves the Assembly, and addresses the first session after each general election.
A bill becomes law only after his signature, and he may give assent, withhold it, or return the bill for reconsideration.
When the legislature is not in session he can promulgate ordinances under Article 213, which must be approved within six months.
Financial powers: the annual budget is presented in his name, and Money Bills are introduced only with his recommendation.
Judicial powers: he appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court and can pardon or commute, except death sentences.
Discretionary powers: he may reserve a bill for the President, call the leader of any party when no party has a majority, and dismiss a ministry that cannot prove its majority.
Under Article 356 he can recommend President's Rule, and Article 361 protects him from answering to any court for his official acts.
